propositions.text: The Court considers and clarifies the Criminal Code regime governing bail pending appeal.
propositions.quote: This appeal provides the Court with an opportunity to consider and clarify the statutory regime in the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , which governs bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Focus on principles guiding appellate courts on bail pending appeal for serious crime convictions with lengthy imprisonment.
propositions.quote: In particular, we are concerned with the principles and policy considerations by which appellate courts should be guided in deciding whether a person, like the appellant Dennis James Oland, who has been convicted of a serious crime and sentenced to a lengthy term of imprisonment, should be released on bail pending the determination of his appeal against conviction.

paragraphs.summary: The Court considers the Criminal Code regime and principles for bail pending appeal for serious crime convictions, focusing on appellant Oland.

propositions.text: The appeal focuses on interpretation and application of Criminal Code ss. 679(3) and 680(1).
propositions.quote: The debate in this appeal focuses on the interpretation and application of two relatively brief provisions of the Code — s. 679(3) and s. 680(1) .

propositions.text: Section 679(3) allows release pending appeal if appellant shows appeal is not frivolous, will surrender, and detention not necessary in public interest.
propositions.quote: 679 . . . (3) In the case of an appeal [against conviction], the judge of the court of appeal may order that the appellant be released pending the determination of his appeal if the appellant establishes that (a) the appeal . . . is not frivolous; (b) he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the order; and (c) his detention is not necessary in the public interest.

propositions.text: Section 680(1) allows review of a judge's bail decision by the court of appeal, which may vary or substitute the decision.
propositions.quote: 680 (1) A decision made by a judge under section . . . 679 may, on the direction of the chief justice or acting chief justice of the court of appeal, be reviewed by that court and that court may, if it does not confirm the decision, (a) vary the decision; or (b) substitute such other decision as, in its opinion, should have been made.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal concerns interpretation of ss. 679(3) and 680(1) of the Criminal Code, which govern bail pending appeal and review of bail decisions.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland applied for bail pending appeal after second degree murder conviction; application denied on public interest ground.
propositions.quote: In the present case, Mr. Oland applied for bail pending appeal following his conviction on a charge of second degree murder involving the death of his father. His application was denied under the public interest criterion set out in s. 679(3) (c).

propositions.text: Appeal judge found public safety not at issue but public confidence in justice would not be maintained if Oland released.
propositions.quote: While public safety was not in issue, the appeal judge was not persuaded that public confidence in the administration of justice would be maintained if Mr. Oland were to be released.

propositions.text: Review panel upheld appeal judge's detention decision as reasonable and free of material error.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the three-judge review panel, the decision of the appeal judge to detain Mr. Oland was “neither unreasonable nor the product of any material error of fact, law or mixed law and fact” (2016 NBCA 15, 446 N.B.R. (2d) 325, at para. 15).

paragraphs.summary: Oland's bail application was denied on public interest grounds; appeal judge and review panel upheld detention decision.

propositions.text: Detaining Oland on public interest grounds was clearly unwarranted in these circumstances.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I am respectfully of the view that detaining Mr. Oland on the public interest criterion was clearly unwarranted in the circumstances.

propositions.text: Appeal judge made a material legal error affecting outcome; review panel erred in not intervening.
propositions.quote: Moreover, in his reasons, the learned appeal judge made a material legal error that affected the outcome. It follows, in my respectful view, that the review panel erred in failing to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Oland's detention unwarranted and that the appeal judge erred legally; review panel erred by not intervening.

propositions.text: Before this Court's hearing, New Brunswick Court of Appeal allowed Oland's conviction appeal and ordered new trial; Oland released on bail pending retrial.
propositions.quote: As it turns out, prior to Mr. Oland’s appeal being argued in this Court, the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick heard and allowed his appeal from conviction and ordered a new trial. In consequence, Mr. Oland was released on bail pending his re-trial.

propositions.text: Oland's appeal to this Court became moot but Court chose to hear it and would allow the appeal with no further order.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, his appeal to this Court from the order of the review panel upholding his detention order was rendered moot. However, for reasons which I will explain, we chose to hear the appeal on its merits — and having done so, we would allow the appeal but make no further order.

paragraphs.summary: Oland's conviction appeal was allowed and bail granted, rendering this appeal moot; Court hears and allows appeal but makes no further order.

propositions.text: On July 7, 2011, Richard Oland was found bludgeoned to death; Dennis Oland became primary suspect and was charged with second degree murder on Nov 12, 2013.
propositions.quote: On July 7, 2011, Mr. Oland’s father, Richard Oland, was found bludgeoned to death at his office in Saint John, New Brunswick. During the ensuing police investigation, Mr. Oland became the primary suspect. He was eventually arrested and charged with second degree murder on November 12, 2013.

paragraphs.summary: Richard Oland was murdered in 2011; Dennis Oland was charged with second degree murder in 2013.

propositions.text: Dennis Oland was released on bail pending trial in 2013; convicted of second degree murder in Dec 2015; sentenced to life with no parole for 10 years in Feb 2016.
propositions.quote: On November 18, 2013, following a contested hearing, Mr. Oland was released on bail pending trial upon entering into a surety recognizance in the amount of $50,000, with conditions. On December 19, 2015, after a three-month trial by judge and jury, he was convicted of second degree murder. On February 11, 2016, the trial judge sentenced him to life imprisonment with no chance of parole for 10 years.

paragraphs.summary: Oland was released on bail in 2013, convicted in 2015, and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2016.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Oland was well-educated, devoted family man with no criminal past and no realistic future danger risk.
propositions.quote: In his sentencing reasons, the trial judge found that apart from the offence for which he now stood convicted, Mr. Oland was “a well-educated 47 year old husband and devoted father without a criminal past”, and “a loving/caring man; a man at the heart of his family and a contributing member of his community” (2016 NBQB 43, 447 N.B.R. (2d) 7, at paras. 14 and 18).

propositions.text: Trial judge found Oland posed no realistic risk of future dangerousness and had excellent reintegration prospects.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the trial judge, Mr. Oland posed no realistic risk of future dangerousness and his prospect of successfully reintegrating into society after serving his sentence was excellent.

propositions.text: Trial judge characterized the offence as brutal but spontaneous outburst from family dysfunction, with lower moral culpability closer to manslaughter.
propositions.quote: As for the offence, the trial judge characterized it as “brutal”, noting approximately 40 blunt and sharp force injuries inflicted to the deceased’s head. On the other hand, the crime involved a spontaneous outburst that was the product of a long-standing dysfunctional family dynamic and immense stress. For this reason, the trial judge found that it fell at the “lower end” on the continuum of moral culpability for second degree murder, closer to manslaughter than to first degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found Oland a devoted family man posing no future danger; offence was brutal but spontaneous with lower moral culpability.

propositions.text: Oland filed notice of appeal from conviction in Jan 2016, advancing grounds on jury charge, evidence admission, and verdict reasonableness; also applied for bail pending appeal.
propositions.quote: On January 20, 2016, Mr. Oland filed a notice of appeal from conviction with the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick. He advanced numerous grounds of appeal relating to three principal areas: errors in the jury charge; errors in admitting certain evidence; and the reasonableness of the verdict. At the same time, he applied under s. 679(3) of the Code for bail pending the determination of his appeal.

propositions.text: The outcome of Oland's bail application is the focus of this appeal.
propositions.quote: The outcome of that application is the focus of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Oland appealed his conviction on multiple grounds and applied for bail pending appeal; bail application outcome is central to this appeal.

propositions.text: Oland's bail application proceeded before a single appeal judge; he filed affidavits on good character, compliance, community roots, sureties, and trial transcript excerpts.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland’s application for release pending appeal proceeded before a single judge of the Court of Appeal. In support of his application, Mr. Oland filed numerous affidavits attesting to his good character, past compliance with release conditions, and his roots in the community. In addition, he filed affidavits from two family members who were prepared to act as sureties and risk substantial sums of money should he breach the terms of his release order. Finally, he submitted excerpts from the trial transcripts pertinent to his grounds of appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Oland supported his bail application with affidavits on character, compliance, sureties, and trial transcript excerpts before a single appeal judge.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found Oland met first two bail criteria: appeal not frivolous and he would surrender as required.
propositions.quote: In ruling on the application, the appeal judge found that Mr. Oland had discharged his onus on the first two criteria for release under s. 679(3)(a) and (b) of the Code, namely: his appeal was not frivolous and he would surrender into custody as required.

propositions.text: Appeal judge considered public interest criterion by dividing it into public safety and public confidence.
propositions.quote: The appeal judge then considered the public interest criterion under s. 679(3) (c), dividing it into two parts — public safety and public confidence in the administration of justice.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal judge found Oland met appeal and surrender criteria, then considered public interest as public safety and public confidence.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found Oland posed no danger to public, adopting sentencing judge's findings of good behaviour and unique family situation.
propositions.quote: Commencing with public safety, the appeal judge was satisfied that Mr. Oland posed “no danger to the public at large” (para. 15). In this regard, he adopted the findings of the sentencing judge that Mr. Oland was a man of prior good behaviour, without criminal record, and that the offence was largely the product of unique relational and situation-specific difficulties existing between him and his father.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal judge found Oland posed no public danger, adopting sentencing judge's findings of good behaviour and unique family context.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found offence gravity and brutality favored detention; grounds of appeal arguable but not strong enough to assure new trial or acquittal.
propositions.quote: Turning to public confidence, the appeal judge found that the gravity and brutality of the offence weighed in favour of Mr. Oland’s detention. And while the grounds of appeal put forward by him were “clearly arguable”, they were not of such unique strength as to “virtually assure a new trial or an acquittal” (paras. 30 and 32).

propositions.text: Appeal judge was not persuaded public confidence in justice would be maintained if Oland released; dismissed bail application.
propositions.quote: On balance, the appeal judge was not persuaded that public confidence in the administration of justice would be maintained if Mr. Oland were to be released. Accordingly, he dismissed the application for release pending appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal judge found offence gravity favored detention and bail would harm public confidence; bail application dismissed.

propositions.text: Chief Justice directed a review of Oland's detention order before a three-judge panel under s. 680(1).
propositions.quote: On application by Mr. Oland under s. 680(1) of the Code, the Chief Justice of New Brunswick directed a review of his detention order before a three-judge panel of the court.

paragraphs.summary: Chief Justice ordered a three-judge panel review of Oland's detention order under s. 680(1).

propositions.text: Review panel adopted deferential approach, viewing detention decision as a judgment call.
propositions.quote: In arriving at its decision, the panel adopted a deferential approach to the review, characterizing the appeal judge’s decision to detain Mr. Oland as a “judgment call”.

propositions.text: Panel recognized Oland's grounds of appeal as serious but noted conviction for brutal murder with mandatory life sentence.
propositions.quote: While the panel recognized that the grounds of appeal put forward by Mr. Oland were “serious”, he nonetheless stood convicted of a brutal murder for which he had received a mandatory life sentence.

propositions.text: Panel found denying bail would not render appeal pointless; no error found in appeal judge's reasons; detention not clearly unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In the circumstances, denying him bail would not render his appeal pointless. Of primary significance, Mr. Oland had failed to show any error in the reasons of the appeal judge that would warrant interference; nor had he persuaded the panel that his detention in the circumstances was clearly unreasonable.

propositions.text: Panel dismissed Oland's application for review of detention order.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the application for review was dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Review panel deferred to appeal judge's detention decision, found no error, and dismissed Oland's review application.

propositions.text: On Oct 24, 2016, New Brunswick Court of Appeal allowed Oland's conviction appeal and ordered new trial; Oct 25, 2016, Oland granted bail pending retrial.
propositions.quote: On October 24, 2016, the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick allowed Mr. Oland’s appeal from conviction and ordered a new trial. On October 25, 2016, he was granted bail pending his re-trial.

propositions.text: Parties were alerted to address mootness issue due to these developments.
propositions.quote: In view of these events, the parties were alerted that they should be prepared to address the issue of mootness.

paragraphs.summary: New Brunswick Court of Appeal allowed Oland's appeal and granted bail, raising mootness issue for this Court.

propositions.text: Court raised mootness issue at hearing start; parties and interveners urged hearing on merits.
propositions.quote: At the commencement of the hearing, the Court raised the issue of mootness and we were urged by the parties and interveners to hear the appeal on its merits.

propositions.text: Oland submitted Court's decision significant as he might face same situation after retrial.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the respondent Crown submitted that this Court’s decision was potentially of significance to them, as Mr. Oland might find himself in the same situation following his re-trial.

propositions.text: All parties submitted guidance needed to resolve inconsistent appellate bail approaches across Canada.
propositions.quote: In addition, all concerned submitted that guidance was needed from this Court to resolve inconsistent approaches to bail taken by appellate courts across the country.

propositions.text: Bail pending appeal is temporary and evasive of appellate review; this case appropriate to resolve conflicting jurisprudence per Borowski and McNeil.
propositions.quote: And as bail pending appeal was, by its temporary nature, evasive of appellate review, this was an appropriate case to resolve the conflicting jurisprudence: see Borowski v. Canada (Attorney General), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342; R. v. McNeil, 2009 SCC 3, [2009] 1 S.C.R. 66, at para. 2.

paragraphs.summary: Court raised mootness; parties urged hearing on merits for guidance on inconsistent bail approaches; case suitable per precedent.

propositions.text: Court decided to hear appeal on merits due to unanimous party position and Borowski criteria met.
propositions.quote: In view of the unanimous position taken by the parties and interveners, and considering that the appeal meets the criteria established in Borowski, the Court determined that it would proceed to hear the appeal on its merits.

paragraphs.summary: Court decided to hear appeal on merits given unanimous party support and Borowski criteria met.

propositions.text: Section 679(3) sets three criteria for bail pending appeal: appeal not frivolous, surrender, and detention not necessary in public interest.
propositions.quote: The three statutory criteria for bail pending appeal are found in s. 679(3) of the Code: 679 . . . (3) In the case of an appeal [against conviction], the judge of the court of appeal may order that the appellant be released pending the determination of his appeal if the appellant establishes that (a) the appeal . . . is not frivolous; (b) he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the order; and (c) his detention is not necessary in the public interest.

propositions.text: Applicant bears burden to prove each criterion on balance of probabilities, citing Ponak, Iyer, D’Amico, and Gill.
propositions.quote: The applicant seeking bail bears the burden of establishing that each criterion is met on a balance of probabilities: R. v. Ponak, [1972] 4 W.W.R. 316 (B.C.C.A.), at pp. 317-18; R. v. Iyer, 2016 ABCA 407, at para. 7 (CanLII); R. v. D’Amico, 2016 QCCA 183, at para. 10 (CanLII); R. v. Gill, 2015 SKCA 96, 465 Sask. R. 253, at para. 14.

paragraphs.summary: Section 679(3) requires appellant to prove appeal not frivolous, surrender, and detention unnecessary; burden is on applicant on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: First criterion requires appeal judge to ensure grounds of appeal are not frivolous; test is a very low bar.
propositions.quote: The first criterion requires the appeal judge to examine the grounds of appeal with a view to ensuring that they are not “not frivolous” (s. 679(3)(a)). Courts have used different language to describe this standard. While not in issue on this appeal, the “not frivolous” test is widely recognized as being a very low bar: see R. v. Xanthoudakis, 2016 QCCA 1809, at paras. 4-7 (CanLII); R. v. Manasseri, 2013 ONCA 647, 312 C.C.C. (3d) 132, at para. 38; R. v. Passey, 1997 ABCA 343, 121 C.C.C. (3d) 444, at paras. 6-8; G. T. Trotter, The Law of Bail in Canada (3rd ed. (loose-leaf)), at pp. 10-13 to 10-15.

paragraphs.summary: The 'not frivolous' appeal criterion is a very low bar requiring appeal judge to examine grounds of appeal.

propositions.text: Applicant must show he will surrender into custody as required under s. 679(3)(b).
propositions.quote: The second criterion requires the applicant to show that “he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the [release] order” (s. 679(3)(b)).

propositions.text: Appeal judge must be satisfied applicant will not flee and will surrender into custody.
propositions.quote: The appeal judge must be satisfied that the applicant will not flee the jurisdiction and will surrender into custody as required.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must show he will surrender into custody and not flee as required by s. 679(3)(b).

propositions.text: Applicant must establish detention is not necessary in the public interest under s. 679(3)(c).
propositions.quote: The third criterion requires the applicant to establish that “his detention is not necessary in the public interest” (s. 679(3)(c)).

propositions.text: Mr. Oland's bail pending appeal failed on the public interest criterion.
propositions.quote: It is upon this criterion that Mr. Oland’s bid for bail pending appeal failed

propositions.text: Parties seek guidance on how strength of grounds of appeal affects public interest detention analysis.
propositions.quote: the parties ask this Court for guidance on how the strength of the grounds of appeal from a conviction should be considered in determining whether detention is necessary in the public interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Oland's bail failed on public interest and parties seek guidance on considering appeal strength in public interest.

propositions.text: In R. v. Farinacci, public interest criterion has two components: public safety and public confidence.
propositions.quote: she determined that the public interest criterion consisted of two components: public safety and public confidence in the administration of justice (pp. 47-48).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision in Farinacci found public interest includes public safety and public confidence components.

propositions.text: Public safety relates to protection of the public and tracks secondary ground for release pending trial.
propositions.quote: She found that it related to the protection and safety of the public and essentially tracked the familiar requirements of the so-called “secondary ground” governing an accused’s release pending trial (pp. 45 and 47-48).

propositions.text: Public confidence involves weighing enforceability and reviewability interests.
propositions.quote: The public confidence component, on the other hand, was more nuanced and required elaboration. It involved the weighing of two competing interests: enforceability and reviewability.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision found public safety concerns protection, while public confidence weighs enforceability and reviewability interests.

propositions.text: Enforceability means respecting immediate enforceability of judgments.
propositions.quote: the enforceability interest reflected the need to respect the general rule of the immediate enforceability of judgments.

propositions.text: Reviewability means society acknowledges justice system is fallible and appeals should be meaningful.
propositions.quote: Reviewability, on the other hand, reflected society’s acknowledgement that our justice system is not infallible and that persons who challenge the legality of their convictions should be entitled to a meaningful review process

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision explained enforceability respects immediate judgments; reviewability acknowledges fallibility and meaningful appeals.

propositions.text: Farinacci's public interest framework has been universally endorsed and remains good law.
propositions.quote: The public interest framework which it established has withstood the test of time. It has been universally endorsed by appellate courts across the country... Farinacci remains good law in my view.

propositions.text: All parties and interveners accept the Farinacci framework and none seek to revisit it.
propositions.quote: all of the parties and interveners in this appeal are content with the Farinacci framework. None has spoken against it; none has asked us to revisit it

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Farinacci's framework is accepted by all parties and remains good law.

propositions.text: Public safety and public confidence components are not silos and should be considered together.
propositions.quote: I should not be taken to mean — nor do I understand Farinacci to have said — that the public safety component and the public confidence component are to be treated as silos.

propositions.text: Residual public safety concerns remain relevant in public confidence analysis even if public safety threshold is met.
propositions.quote: where the public safety threshold has been met by an applicant seeking bail pending appeal, residual public safety concerns or the absence of any public safety concerns remain relevant and should be considered in the public confidence analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies public safety and confidence components overlap and residual safety concerns affect public confidence analysis.

propositions.text: Difficulty arises in applying Farinacci when balancing enforceability and reviewability in serious crime and strong bail candidate cases.
propositions.quote: Appellate judges continue to have difficulty resolving the tension between enforceability and reviewability, especially in cases like the present one, where they are faced with a serious crime on the one hand, and a strong candidate for bail pending appeal on the other.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellate judges struggle balancing enforceability and reviewability in serious crime and strong bail cases.

propositions.text: Public confidence component rarely plays a central role in bail pending appeal decisions.
propositions.quote: Rarely does this component play a role, much less a central role, in the decision to grant or deny bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Porisky observed not every offence is serious enough to engage public confidence assessment.
propositions.quote: Not every offence is serious enough to engage an assessment of the merits. There is no need to go beyond the frivolous threshold in cases unlikely to arouse a concern about public confidence.

propositions.text: Crown counsel should raise public confidence only in serious offences.
propositions.quote: we should expect Crown counsel to recognize that the continuum runs from petty theft to first degree murder and to exercise good judgment in raising public confidence only in those cases where the offence is at the serious end of the scale.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes public confidence rarely central; Porisky says only serious offences warrant public confidence concerns.

propositions.text: The court will elaborate on enforceability and reviewability interests to guide appellate judges.
propositions.quote: I propose to elaborate somewhat on the competing interests of enforceability and reviewability identified in Farinacci.

paragraphs.summary: The court proposes to elaborate on enforceability and reviewability interests to assist appellate judges.

propositions.text: Parliament has not provided direction on public confidence in release pending appeal orders under s. 679(3)(c).
propositions.quote: In section 679(3)(c) of the Code, Parliament has not provided appellate judges with any direction as to how a release pending appeal order is likely to affect public confidence in the administration of justice.

propositions.text: Parliament identified four factors in s. 515(10)(c) for bail pending trial to maintain public confidence.
propositions.quote: Under s. 515(10)(c), Parliament has identified four factors that judges may consider in assessing whether a detention order is necessary to maintain public confidence in the administration of justice: ...

propositions.text: The four factors are strength of prosecution's case, gravity of offence, circumstances of offence, and potential length of imprisonment.
propositions.quote: (i) the apparent strength of the prosecution’s case, (ii) the gravity of the offence, (iii) the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, including whether a firearm was used, and (iv) the fact that the accused is liable, on conviction, for a potentially lengthy term of imprisonment

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Parliament gave four factors for bail pending trial public confidence in s. 515(10)(c), but none for appeal context.

propositions.text: The four bail pending trial factors should be adapted for bail pending appeal public confidence analysis.
propositions.quote: these same factors — with appropriate modifications to reflect the post-conviction context — should be accounted for in considering how, if at all, a release pending appeal order is likely to affect public confidence

paragraphs.summary: The court argues bail pending trial factors should be adapted for bail pending appeal public confidence analysis.

propositions.text: Using the same factors promotes consistency and fairness between trial and appellate bail contexts.
propositions.quote: It has the virtue of promoting consistency and harmony between the trial and appellate contexts so that, together, they may be seen as providing a cohesive and comprehensive statement of the law governing bail in Canada.

propositions.text: Bail should not be more accessible after conviction than before trial to foster fairness and public confidence.
propositions.quote: it accords with the basic principle that, in general, bail should not be more readily accessible for someone who has been convicted of a crime than for someone who is awaiting trial and is presumed innocent.

paragraphs.summary: The court says adapting factors promotes consistency and fairness, ensuring bail is not easier after conviction than before trial.

propositions.text: Accused persons are presumed innocent and have a right to reasonable bail under s. 11(e) of the Charter.
propositions.quote: Accused persons charged with an offence in Canada are presumed to be innocent, and they remain so unless and until their guilt is proved beyond a reasonable doubt. ... s. 11 (e) the right of every person charged with an offence “not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains accused persons have presumption of innocence and right to reasonable bail under s. 11(e) of the Charter.

propositions.text: After conviction, presumption of innocence and s. 11(e) no longer apply; onus shifts to applicant for bail pending appeal.
propositions.quote: once a conviction is entered, the presumption of innocence is displaced and s. 11 (e) of the Charter no longer applies. ... Parliament has seen fit to reverse the onus onto the applicant in all cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that after conviction, presumption of innocence ends and onus for bail pending appeal is on applicant.

propositions.text: The court will explain how s. 515(10)(c) factors inform public confidence component in s. 679(3)(c).
propositions.quote: I turn to the enforceability and reviewability interests to explain how, with appropriate modifications, the public confidence factors listed in s. 515(10)(c) are instructive

paragraphs.summary: The court will explain how s. 515(10)(c) factors inform public confidence in s. 679(3)(c).

propositions.text: Seriousness of crime affects public confidence in bail pending trial and should equally affect enforceability interest in bail pending appeal.
propositions.quote: In assessing whether public confidence concerns support a pre-trial detention order ... the seriousness of the crime plays an important role. ... So too for bail pending appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court says seriousness of crime affects public confidence in bail pending trial and appeal enforceability interest equally.

propositions.text: Parliament's three factors for seriousness of crime in s. 515(10)(c) apply to s. 679(3)(c) with trial judge's sentencing reasons available.
propositions.quote: these factors are readily transferable to s. 679(3)(c) — the only difference being ... the appeal judge will generally have the trial judge’s reasons for sentence

paragraphs.summary: The court says Parliament's three seriousness factors apply to s. 679(3)(c) with trial judge's sentencing reasons.

propositions.text: Other factors like residual public safety or flight risks remain relevant under public confidence and can tip scale for detention.
propositions.quote: public safety concerns that fall short of the substantial risk mark ... will remain relevant under the public confidence component and can, in some cases, tip the scale in favour of detention

propositions.text: Absence of flight or public safety risks attenuates enforceability interest.
propositions.quote: The same holds true for lingering flight risks that do not rise to the substantial risk level ... By the same token, the absence of flight or public safety risks will attenuate the enforceability interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court says residual public safety or flight risks affect public confidence; absence of such risks reduces enforceability interest.

propositions.text: Strength of prosecution's case in s. 515(10)(c) translates to strength of grounds of appeal in appellate context and is central to reviewability interest.
propositions.quote: The remaining factor ... is the strength of the prosecution’s case ... In the appellate context, this translates into the strength of the grounds of appeal — and ... the strength of an appeal plays a central role.

propositions.text: Concerns about assessing appeal merits beyond 'not frivolous' criterion are not problematic.
propositions.quote: some authorities have expressed concerns about assessing the merits of an appeal beyond the s. 679(3)(a) “not frivolous” criterion ... With respect, I do not see this as a problem.

paragraphs.summary: The court says strength of grounds of appeal is central to reviewability and concerns about assessing merits beyond 'not frivolous' are unfounded.

propositions.text: The 'not frivolous' criterion in s. 679(3)(a) is an initial hurdle producing a categorical yes or no answer.
propositions.quote: allowing a more pointed consideration of the strength of an appeal for purposes of assessing the reviewability interest does not render the “not frivolous” criterion in s. 679(3)(a) meaningless. On the contrary, the “not frivolous” criterion operates as an initial hurdle that produces a categorical “yes” or “no” answer

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 'not frivolous' criterion in s. 679(3)(a) is an initial hurdle producing a categorical yes or no answer.

propositions.text: Justice Donald in Porisky says 'not frivolous' and 'sufficient merit' do not foreclose merits consideration beyond threshold test.
propositions.quote: The express mention of “not frivolous” in s. 679(3)(a) and “sufficient merit” in s. 679(4) (a) does not, in my view, foreclose consideration of the merits for a purpose other than a threshold test.

propositions.text: The court agrees with Justice Donald that merits can be considered beyond threshold test for public interest limits.
propositions.quote: Once over the threshold, the applicant faces the question of the public interest, a phrase not defined in the legislation but which had to be given some limits if it was to survive constitutional scrutiny. That is what Farinacci did.

propositions.text: Farinacci set boundaries for public interest criterion using merits assessment differently than threshold test.
propositions.quote: In setting boundaries for the public interest criterion, in particular the public confidence element, Farinacci employed the merits assessment for a purpose different from the threshold test.

propositions.text: No redundancy or doubt about authority to consider merits as part of public confidence question.
propositions.quote: So I see no redundancy; nor do I doubt our authority to consider the merits as part of the public confidence question.

propositions.text: See also R. v. Delisle for similar reasoning.
propositions.quote: See also: R. v. Delisle, 2012 QCCA 1250, at paras. 4 and 52 (CanLII).

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Justice Donald in Porisky and Farinacci that merits can be considered beyond threshold test for public interest limits.

propositions.text: Gary T. Trotter explains serious offences require more probing inquiry into chances of success on appeal.
propositions.quote: when an offence is serious, as with murder cases, such that public concern about enforceability is ignited, there should be a more probing inquiry into the chances of success on appeal.

propositions.text: Balancing required by Farinacci requires merits assessment separate from threshold test.
propositions.quote: It is in this context that the balancing required by Farinacci requires some assessment of the merits, separate from the question of whether the appeal is frivolous or not.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Gary T. Trotter that serious offences require probing inquiry into appeal chances, with merits assessment separate from threshold test.

propositions.text: Appellate judges assess grounds of appeal for legal plausibility and record foundation to surpass 'not frivolous' criterion.
propositions.quote: appellate judges will examine the grounds identified in the notice of appeal with an eye to their general legal plausibility and their foundation in the record

propositions.text: Avoid categories and grading schemes like 'prospect of success' as they are unhelpful and complex.
propositions.quote: categories and grading schemes should be avoided. Phrases such as “a prospect of success”, “a moderate prospect of success”, or “a realistic prospect of success” are generally not helpful.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules appellate judges assess grounds for legal plausibility to surpass 'not frivolous' and avoid unhelpful grading schemes.

propositions.text: Appellate judges form preliminary assessment of appeal strength based on counsel material and record, not guesswork.
propositions.quote: appellate judges can be counted on to form their own “preliminary assessment” of the strength of an appeal based upon their knowledge and experience...not a matter of guesswork

propositions.text: Review process essential to maintain public confidence in justice administration, transcending individual interest.
propositions.quote: a meaningful review process is essential to maintain public confidence in the administration of justice. Thus, there is a broader public interest in reviewability that transcends an individual’s interest in any given case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellate judges form preliminary assessments based on counsel and record, essential to maintain public confidence beyond individual interest.

propositions.text: Remedy sought on appeal may inform reviewability interest; e.g., reducing murder to manslaughter lessens reviewability.
propositions.quote: if a successful appeal can result only in a murder conviction being reduced to manslaughter, this will lessen the interest in reviewability

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting that remedy affects reviewability interest.
propositions.quote: R. v. Meda (1981)...R. v. Olsen (1996)...R. v. Roe, 2008 BCCA 253...R. v. Lees, 1999 BCCA 441

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the remedy sought on appeal may lessen reviewability interest, citing supporting cases.

propositions.text: Appellate judges must evaluate public confidence factors through eyes of reasonable, informed, dispassionate public member.
propositions.quote: public confidence is to be measured through the eyes of a reasonable member of the public...thoughtful, dispassionate, informed of the circumstances of the case and respectful of society’s fundamental values

propositions.text: Distinguish public confidence from uninformed public opinion, which has no role in bail decisions.
propositions.quote: public confidence in the administration of justice must be distinguished from uninformed public opinion about the case, which has no role to play in the decision to grant bail or not.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules appellate judges evaluate public confidence through a reasonable public lens, excluding uninformed opinion.

propositions.text: Appellate judges should consider sentence length and appeal delay when balancing enforceability and reviewability.
propositions.quote: appellate judges should also be mindful of the anticipated delay in deciding an appeal, relative to the length of the sentence

propositions.text: If bail is impossible and delay is long, judges should consider expediting appeal under s. 679(10).
propositions.quote: where a bail order is out of the question, appellate judges should consider ordering the appeal expedited under s. 679(10) of the Code

paragraphs.summary: The court rules appellate judges consider sentence length and appeal delay, and may expedite appeals if bail is impossible.

propositions.text: No precise formula exists to balance enforceability and reviewability; qualitative, contextual assessment required.
propositions.quote: there is no precise formula that can be applied to resolve the balance between enforceability and reviewability. A qualitative and contextual assessment is required.

propositions.text: Reject categorical approach to murder or serious offences; apply principles uniformly.
propositions.quote: I would reject a categorical approach to murder or other serious offences, as proposed by certain interveners. Instead, the principles that I have discussed should be applied uniformly.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules no precise formula exists; qualitative assessment needed and categorical approaches to serious offences rejected.

propositions.text: For murder or serious crimes, public interest in enforceability is high and often outweighs reviewability, especially with safety or flight concerns or weak grounds.
propositions.quote: where the applicant has been convicted of murder or some other very serious crime, the public interest in enforceability will be high and will often outweigh the reviewability interest, particularly where there are lingering public safety or flight concerns and/or the grounds of appeal appear to be weak

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting high enforceability interest in serious crimes.
propositions.quote: R. v. Mapara, 2001 BCCA 508...Baltovich...Parsons

paragraphs.summary: The court rules enforceability interest is high and often outweighs reviewability in serious crimes with safety or flight concerns or weak grounds.

propositions.text: Where safety or flight concerns negligible and grounds surpass 'not frivolous', reviewability may outweigh enforceability even in serious offences.
propositions.quote: where public safety or flight concerns are negligible, and where the grounds of appeal clearly surpass the “not frivolous” criterion, the public interest in reviewability may well overshadow the enforceability interest, even in the case of murder or other very serious offences.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules that negligible safety or flight concerns and strong grounds may make reviewability outweigh enforceability even in serious offences.

propositions.text: Before applying principles, court will address principles governing review hearing under s. 680(1).
propositions.quote: Before applying these principles to the case at hand, I propose to address the principles that govern a review hearing under s. 680(1) of the Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court will next address principles governing review hearing under s. 680(1) before applying prior principles.

propositions.text: s. 680(1) is a review mechanism for orders under s. 679(3) and certain pre-trial bail orders including murder.
propositions.quote: s. 680(1) of the Code operates as a review mechanism for an order of a single judge of the Court of Appeal made under s. 679(3)...applies as well to certain pre-trial bail orders made by superior court judges for various offences, including murder.

propositions.text: s. 680(1) allows court to vary or substitute decisions on review.
propositions.quote: that court may, if it does not confirm the decision, (a) vary the decision; or (b) substitute such other decision as, in its opinion, should have been made.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 680(1) reviews orders under s. 679(3) and pre-trial bail, allowing variation or substitution of decisions.

propositions.text: Review process under s. 680(1) has two stages: chief justice vetting and court review if directed.
propositions.quote: the review process consists of two stages: first, an initial vetting by the chief justice; and second, a review by the court, if directed by the chief justice.

propositions.text: Review usually conducted by a three-judge panel, as in this case.
propositions.quote: In practice, the review will generally be conducted by a panel of three judges, as it was in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 680(1) review has two stages: chief justice vetting and panel review, usually by three judges.

propositions.text: Chief justice's screening considers review nature and standard to be applied by panel.
propositions.quote: The nature of the review and the standard to be applied by the panel...are factors that the chief justice is likely to take into account in carrying out his or her initial screening function.

propositions.text: Court finds it useful to address panel's mandate before chief justice's screening function.
propositions.quote: I find it useful to address the review panel’s mandate before addressing the chief justice’s screening function.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes chief justice's screening considers review nature and standard; court will address panel mandate first.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 680(1) panel review should apply correctness standard with robust review.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the intervener Criminal Lawyers’ Association (Ontario) (“CLA”) submit that a standard of correctness should apply, meaning that the panel should engage in a robust review of the record and come to its own independent determination

propositions.text: Crown and Attorneys General argue for deferential standard requiring legal error before intervention.
propositions.quote: The respondent Crown and the Attorneys General of Ontario and Alberta submit that a more deferential standard is appropriate — one in which an error of law or principle must be found before intervention will be warranted.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue for correctness standard on s. 680(1) review; Crown and Attorneys General argue for deferential standard.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue absence of 'show cause' in s. 680(1) implies less deferential review than at trial stage.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the CLA make two main submissions. First, they point to ss. 520 and 521 of the Code...absence of similar language in s. 680(1)...should be interpreted as invoking a less deferential standard

propositions.text: St-Cloud observed 'show cause' signals less interventionist approach at trial stage; absence in s. 680(1) noted.
propositions.quote: In St-Cloud, this Court observed that the words “show cause” signal a less interventionist, more deferential approach to bail reviews at the trial stage...noted the absence of similar language in s. 680(1)

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue absence of 'show cause' in s. 680(1) implies less deferential review; St-Cloud noted 'show cause' signals deferential approach at trial.

propositions.text: Court rejects argument that absence of 'show cause' means less deferential review under s. 680(1).
propositions.quote: I would not give effect to this argument. While the words “show cause” are not found in s. 680(1), I am not convinced that their absence is as significant as Mr. Oland and the CLA suggest.

propositions.text: Expected more explicit language if Parliament intended panel to substitute opinion without more.
propositions.quote: I would have expected more explicit language than the language used in s. 680(1), if Parliament intended the review to be a process in which the panel could, without more, simply substitute its opinion for that of the judge.

propositions.text: In St-Cloud, Court stated comments not determinative of review type under s. 680(1).
propositions.quote: in St-Cloud, at para. 104, Wagner J. for the Court stated that his comments were not determinative of the type of review contemplated by s. 680(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects that absence of 'show cause' means less deferential review under s. 680(1), noting St-Cloud comments not determinative.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c) depends on robust correctness review.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the CLA submit that the constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c) hinges on the existence of a robust correctness review.

propositions.text: They rely on Farinacci where Arbour J.A. said correctness standard allows assessment of individual decisions.
propositions.quote: They base this submission on an excerpt from Farinacci, where Arbour J.A. stated...it is a standard against which the correctness of individual decisions can be assessed.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 679(3)(c) constitutionality depends on robust correctness review, citing Farinacci.

propositions.text: Court finds Farinacci reference unpersuasive as it concerned constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c), not review standard here.
propositions.quote: I do not find this reference to be persuasive. In Farinacci, the Court of Appeal was focused on the constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c), a matter that does not concern us in this appeal.

propositions.text: Correctness is not the only meaningful review form protecting against vagueness; review nature here not settled.
propositions.quote: it does not follow that the nature of that review must invoke a correctness standard along the lines suggested by Mr. Oland and the CLA...comments of the Court of Appeal are not dispositive in settling the nature of review contemplated under s. 680(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Farinacci reference unpersuasive and that correctness is not the only meaningful review form; review nature not settled here.

propositions.text: A panel reviewing a s. 680(1) decision should follow three principles: defer to fact findings absent palpable error, intervene for material legal errors, and intervene if decision is clearly unwarranted.
propositions.quote: a panel reviewing a decision of a single judge under s. 680(1) should be guided by the following three principles. First, absent palpable and overriding error, the review panel must show deference to the judge’s findings of fact. Second, the review panel may intervene and substitute its decision for that of the judge where it is satisfied that the judge erred in law or in principle, and the error was material to the outcome. Third, in the absence of legal error, the review panel may intervene and substitute its decision for that of the judge where it concludes that the decision was clearly unwarranted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states three principles guiding review panels under s. 680(1): defer to facts, intervene for material legal errors, and intervene if decision is clearly unwarranted.

propositions.text: This approach balances meaningful review with deference and aligns review standards for serious and non-serious offences under the Code.
propositions.quote: This approach allows for meaningful review while extending a measure of deference to the judge’s decision. It also achieves symmetry with the review process at the trial stage, save for those offences identified in s. 469 of the Code, for which the review process is governed by s. 680(1). This symmetry is important because, as Gary T. Trotter explains in The Law of Bail in Canada, it avoids an anomaly that would otherwise result: Focusing on the review of pre-trial bail orders, endorsing a correctness standard in the application of s. 680 creates differential standards of review for s. 469 vs. non-469 offences. It will allow a more generous scope of review in respect of the most serious offences in the Criminal Code . . . . There is no principled reason that supports a situation where someone detained on a murder charge enjoys a broader scope of review under s. 680 when compared to a person charged with manslaughter or attempted murder (both non-s. 469 offences) who is dealt with under the narrower s. 520 . [p. 8-31] (2) The Chief Justice’s Discretion to Direct a Review

paragraphs.summary: The court explains this approach balances review and deference and ensures consistent standards for serious and non-serious offences.

propositions.text: No formal Code procedure governs the chief justice's decision to direct a panel review; courts vary in approach and formality.
propositions.quote: There is no formal procedure in the Code governing the chief justice’s decision to direct a panel review. We are told that courts of appeal have adopted different approaches and levels of formality.

propositions.text: Procedural aspects of the chief justice's gatekeeping function are not before the court and will not be addressed.
propositions.quote: The procedural aspects of the gatekeeping function are not before us and I do not propose to address them.

propositions.text: Some guidance can be given on the test the chief justice should apply when deciding to direct a panel review.
propositions.quote: Some guidance can, however, be given as to the test a chief justice should apply in deciding whether to direct a panel review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no formal procedure governs the chief justice's panel review decision but offers guidance on the test to apply.

propositions.text: The chief justice should direct a review if it is arguable the judge made material factual or legal errors or the decision was clearly unwarranted.
propositions.quote: The test, as I see it, should be relatively straightforward in its application. It flows from the principles the panel is required to apply when conducting a review. In short, the chief justice should consider directing a review where it is arguable that the judge committed material errors of fact or law in arriving at the impugned decision, or that the impugned decision was clearly unwarranted in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the chief justice should direct a review if material errors or a clearly unwarranted decision are arguable.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland was an ideal bail candidate aside from the offence seriousness; notoriety and public opinion were rightly ignored by the appeal judge.
propositions.quote: By all accounts, aside from the seriousness of the offence for which Mr. Oland was convicted, he presented as an ideal candidate for bail. The notoriety of this case, which stemmed largely from his prominence in the community, and any uninformed public opinion about it, were rightly ignored by the appeal judge. Mr. Oland, I emphasize, was entitled to the same treatment as someone less prominent.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Oland was an ideal bail candidate except for offence seriousness; notoriety was rightly ignored by the appeal judge.

propositions.text: If Mr. Oland did not qualify for release, no one convicted of similarly serious offences would be released without unique or strong appeal grounds.
propositions.quote: there is considerable merit to Mr. Oland’s submission that if he did not qualify for release, no one convicted of a similarly serious offence would ever be released, absent a showing of unique or exceptionally strong grounds of appeal.

propositions.text: Parliament did not restrict bail pending appeal for serious crimes; courts should respect this and consider reviewability over enforceability interests.
propositions.quote: Parliament did not restrict the availability of bail pending appeal for persons convicted of murder or any other serious crime and courts should respect this. Thus, for the purposes of s. 679(3)(c), even in the case of very serious offences, where there are no public safety or flight concerns and the grounds of appeal clearly surpass the “not frivolous” criterion, a court may well conclude that the reviewability interest overshadows the enforceability interest such that detention will not be necessary in the public interest.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues serious offenders should not be categorically denied release; the court agrees bail pending appeal is not restricted for serious crimes.

propositions.text: Each case requires contextual analysis considering factors like criminal record, public safety, flight risk, and release plan strength.
propositions.quote: Every case is different and there may be operative factors in other cases, such as a prior criminal record, public safety and flight risk concerns, or a weaker release plan, which could raise concerns warranting detention. Emphatically, a contextual analysis that can account for these differences is required.

paragraphs.summary: The court states bail decisions require contextual analysis of factors like criminal record, safety, flight risk, and release plan.

propositions.text: The appeal judge found no public safety or flight risk concerns and grounds of appeal were clearly arguable.
propositions.quote: the appeal judge was satisfied that there were no appreciable public safety or flight risk concerns and the grounds of appeal were “clearly arguable”

propositions.text: The appeal judge overlooked the trial judge's finding that the crime gravitated more toward manslaughter, lessening moral blameworthiness and enforceability interest.
propositions.quote: the appeal judge overlooked what I consider to be an important finding made by the trial judge, namely, that in the circumstances, Mr. Oland’s crime gravitated more toward the offence of manslaughter than to first degree murder. This finding was important because it served to lessen Mr. Oland’s degree of moral blameworthiness, thereby attenuating the seriousness of the crime and hence the enforceability interest.

propositions.text: Considering these factors, Mr. Oland’s detention was clearly unwarranted and the Court of Appeal erred in not intervening.
propositions.quote: In my view, the cumulative effect of these considerations ought to have tipped the scale in favour of release. In other words, Mr. Oland’s detention was clearly unwarranted and the Court of Appeal erred in failing to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal judge found no safety or flight risk concerns; the court finds he overlooked manslaughter finding and that detention was clearly unwarranted.

propositions.text: The appeal judge required more than clearly arguable grounds, seeking unique circumstances assuring new trial or acquittal.
propositions.quote: he required more, something in the nature of unique circumstances that would have virtually assured a new trial or an acquittal

propositions.text: The appeal judge erred by requiring more than clearly arguable grounds to assess appeal strength and implications.
propositions.quote: Respectfully, he erred in this regard. That Mr. Oland’s grounds were “clearly arguable” was enough to establish that they clearly surpassed the “not frivolous” criterion.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal judge erred by requiring unique circumstances beyond clearly arguable grounds to assess appeal strength.

propositions.text: Had the appeal not been moot, the court would have set aside detention and ordered release pending appeal; now it allows appeal with no further order.
propositions.quote: In the result, had intervening events not rendered the appeal moot, I would have set aside Mr. Oland’s detention order and ordered his release pending appeal. However, because the appeal is moot, I would simply allow the appeal and make no further order. Appeal allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court would have ordered Mr. Oland's release pending appeal but allows the appeal with no further order due to mootness.
